title: Min-Cost Root-to-Leaf in N-ary Tree
statement:
You are given an n-ary tree with `n` nodes numbered `0` to `n - 1`. Node `0` is the root. Every node `i` carries an integer value `value[i]`, which may be negative, and a node may have any number of children.

The **cost** of a root-to-leaf path is the sum of the values of all nodes on the path, including the root and the leaf. A **leaf** is a node with no children (if `n = 1`, the root itself is the only leaf).

The tree is described by `n - 1` undirected edges; the parent-child direction is determined by the root. Find the minimum cost over all root-to-leaf paths.

Every root-to-leaf path has at most `5000` nodes, so a recursive solution is safe in every language.

**Follow-up:** also return the path itself (the sequence of nodes) that achieves the minimum cost.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers `value[0] ... value[n-1]`.
Each of the next `n - 1` lines contains two integers `u v`, an edge of the tree (0-indexed, either order).
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the minimum root-to-leaf path cost.
constraints: Every root-to-leaf path contains at most 5000 nodes

examples.explanation: Node 0 has children 1, 3 and 4; node 1 has child 2. Leaves: 2, 3, 4. Costs: 10-4-6 = 0, 10+7 = 17, 10+1 = 11. The minimum is 0.

hints: Define best(v) as the cheapest cost of a path that starts at v and ends in a leaf of v's subtree.
For a leaf best(v) = value[v]. Otherwise best(v) = value[v] + the minimum best(c) over the children c of v.
Root the tree at node 0 by traversing from it (children are neighbours other than the one you came from). The answer is best(0). Remember values can be negative, so you cannot stop a path early.
